intro: AI tools for medical billers and coders on a Mac mostly help with the work around your claim software. They explain denial codes, draft appeal letters, read payer portals and keep your trackers tidy. They do not submit claims, post payments or pick codes for you. This guide shows where each tool fits, and where a person must check.
tldr: Some billing apps are Windows-only, including Tebra's desktop app. Check your system requirements before you plan around a Mac.
Use AI to explain, draft and track. Keep code selection, claim submission and payment posting with trained staff.
Denials cost real money to rework. Vendor sources cite about $25 per rework and $118 per appeal.
Do not paste patient identifiers into any AI tool unless your employer's rules allow it.
Lazur looks at your screen only while you hold ⌥⌘. It guides you one click at a time and never clicks for you.

blocks.text: Where a medical biller's day goes

The blog 'A normal day in the life of a Medical Biller' says billers usually work 40 hours per week. It says they spend most of that time in front of a computer. Its task list includes building claims in software, entering codes and patient details, and sending claims through a clearinghouse. It also covers fixing clearinghouse errors, reviewing EOBs and handling denials.

The work is a chain, not a single task. A claim goes out. A payer answers. A payment or a denial comes back, and someone has to post it. Each link has its own screen, its own login and its own rules. That is where most of the friction sits.
Is medical billing a shrinking job?

The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts 418,000 billing and posting clerks in 2025. It projects essentially no change through 2035. BLS also says automated invoice processing software will raise productivity and reduce growth. BLS does not list medical billers as their own group, so treat these figures as a close proxy.

For you, the repeat work is the part most likely to change. Tools handle repetitive text and lookups well. Judgment on payer rules and denial patterns still needs a person who reads the policy and knows the account.
What the numbers on billing time can and cannot tell you

No published study has timed medical billers task by task. The numbers in this guide come from physician surveys, a prior authorization survey and vendor reports. Use them to see the direction of the work. Do not use them as a time study of your own office.
Which AI tools fit the work on a Mac

Most AI tools live in a chat window. Billing work happens across several screens at once. So the useful question is which screen the AI can help with. The table shows how common tasks split across Mac apps.

Points at filters and formulas, and explains the results
Drafts the text, and you check every line before it goes out
Runs research in its own Chrome tabs and returns a summary
Guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click

Medical billing software for Mac: check it before you buy

This step is where Mac billers get stuck. Tebra formed in November 2021 when Kareo and PatientPop merged. Its help center describes the Desktop Application as a native Windows application. It lists Windows 10 or 11 as the operating system. For Macs, it offers a companion solution, and its help page says to contact Customer Care for it.

Check the current help page before you assume anything. Vendors change their requirements. Your practice may also run a Mac companion, a browser version or a remote Windows desktop. Ask your billing vendor which one you use.

Lazur can see any window on your Mac screen, including Chrome. Many clearinghouses, payer portals and EMR lookups run in a browser. Those screens are in reach. A program on a Windows PC is not. Lazur cannot see that screen.

Ask three questions before you rely on any tool. Which screen does the work happen on? Does that screen run on a Mac? Who owns the data you type into it? If you cannot answer the first two, ask your billing vendor or IT lead.
AI for medical coding: where the answer stops

Coders ask AI to explain a code, a modifier or a documentation rule. That can save time on a hard question. An explanation is not a coding decision. Your code set, the payer's policy and your coding guidelines decide the answer.
AI tools can be wrong. They may not know your payer's latest update. Use the tool as a study partner. Ask it why two codes differ, then check the official source before you change a claim.

items: Describe the situation in plain words, and leave out patient identifiers.
Ask why a code fits, and what would make it wrong.
Open the official code book or the payer policy and read the section yourself.
Write the source in the account note before you change the claim.

blocks.title: Do not code from a chat answer
blocks.text: A chat answer is not a source. Your code set and the payer's policy are. Check each code against them before the claim leaves your desk.
Denial management AI tools: triage, appeal and the account note

Denials are where AI tools earn their keep. The queue is long, repetitive and full of similar reason codes. Waystar cites MGMA for about $25 per denial rework. It cites Becker's for $118 to appeal a denied claim.
Waystar also cites an HFMA-linked study. It says 63% of denials are preventable, yet most are never reworked. Triage matters more than speed for that reason. Work the claims you can win first.

Sort the queue by dollar value and by age. Drop the claims the policy does not support. Then decide which denial reasons you will fix at the front desk next time. The same reason code often means the same front-end mistake.
A worked example: one denial from start to appeal

Say a payer denies a claim with a reason code you have not seen this month. Open your denial tracker in Excel. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask Lazur to explain the code on screen. It answers out loud in plain language. Then open the payer's policy in the portal and read it yourself.

Next, draft the appeal. Ask Lazur to draft a short letter in Word with the facts you already have. Remove patient identifiers first. Read every line before you send it. The letter goes out under your practice's name, so the words are yours to check.

Then log the outcome. Hold fn and dictate a short account note with the date, the payer contact, what you asked for and when you will follow up. Dictation puts clean text at the cursor, so the note lands in the right field.

items: Sort by dollar value, then by how old the denial is.
Explain any reason code you do not know, then check the policy.
Draft the appeal only when the policy supports it.
Dictate the account note before you move to the next claim.

blocks.text: Prior authorization and insurer calls

The AMA 2025 Prior Authorization Physician Survey covered 1,000 physicians. It found an average of 40 prior authorizations per physician per week. It found prior authorization takes an average of 13 hours of physician and staff time per week. Staff are dedicated to it exclusively at 40% of physicians.
These are physician practice figures, not biller figures. Use them to understand the pressure on the office. Do not use them to size your own workload.

Insurer calls are where a morning disappears. Keep a call log in Excel with the date, the call reference and the name of the representative. Dictate the call while it is fresh. Ask Lazur to point at the fields you need, one at a time.
Patient data: what you should not paste into an AI tool

Patient information needs the most care. Follow your employer's rules on patient data before you use any AI tool near a claim. Those rules decide what you can paste, dictate or ask about. This page does not make compliance claims for Lazur or any other tool. Ask your compliance lead whether a tool is approved.

Lazur looks at your screen and listens only while you hold the shortcut. The audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. That is the product's stated behavior, and it does not replace your employer's approval.
A claim screen holds names, dates of birth, member IDs and account numbers. Hide the patient columns before you ask a question. Ask about the field or the rule, not about the person.

items: Check that your employer allows AI tools near patient data.
Remove names, dates of birth and member IDs from anything you paste.
Ask about the code or the rule, not the patient.
Close windows that show patient details you do not need.
Tell your compliance lead when a tool does something unexpected.

blocks.text: Setting up Lazur for billing work on a Mac

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Download the app from /download. Open it and approve the macOS permissions it asks for. Then hold ⌥⌘ and ask about the window in front of you.

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Add payer names and abbreviations to your personal dictionary, so dictation gets them right. Use snippets for phrases you repeat, and clipboard slots for reference numbers you keep retyping.
Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on the Mac. Ask Lazur to walk you through where that memory lives. It helps when you want to find last week's question about a payer.
For the Excel side, read [Excel for medical billers on Mac](/for/medical-billers/excel). For mail templates and denial email, read [Outlook for medical billers on Mac](/for/medical-billers/outlook).
Mistakes billers make with AI tools
Most mistakes come from trusting speed. These are the common ones.

items: Treating a chat answer as a payer rule. Check the portal or the policy document.
Pasting a full claim with patient identifiers into any tool. Trim it first.
Letting a tool choose a code. You or your coder choose it, with the source open.
Sending an appeal without reading the letter. You own what leaves the office.
Skipping the account note. A good call with no note is a call you will repeat.
Buying a tool before checking whether the billing app runs on your Mac.

blocks.text: Use reminders for follow-up dates too. Ask Lazur to set a reminder, and it goes into Apple Reminders. A follow-up you forget keeps a denial open longer than it should.
Where to go next

Start small. Pick one repeat task this week, such as denial triage or call notes. Use Lazur on that task for the full week. Then decide whether it saved you time. If it did, add the next task. If not, drop it.

Read the app pages for the screens you use most. Start with [Lazur for Excel](/apps/excel), [Lazur for Outlook](/apps/outlook) and [Lazur for Chrome](/apps/chrome). When you are ready, compare [pricing](/pricing) and [download Lazur](/download).

faq.question: Is there one AI tool for medical billers and coders on Mac?
faq.answer: No single tool covers claim software, clearinghouses, payer portals and coding references. Most billers combine their billing system with a general assistant. Lazur is a general voice assistant for the Mac. It works in any app on screen, and it is not a billing system.

faq.question: Can Lazur submit claims, post payments or change codes for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur explains, points, guides, dictates and drafts text. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You submit the claim, post the payment and choose the code.

faq.question: Can I use AI for medical coding?
faq.answer: You can use AI to explain a code description or a documentation rule. Then check the official code book and the payer policy. An AI answer is not a source you can cite on a claim.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with billing software that only runs on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS only. It sees what is on your Mac screen. A billing program running on a separate Windows PC is outside its view. Windows support is planned, not available.

faq.question: Can I paste patient information into Lazur?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on patient data first. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts do not replace your employer's approval.

faq.question: How do I use Lazur for denial appeals on Mac?
faq.answer: Hold ⌥⌘ and ask Lazur to explain the reason code on screen. Ask it to draft the letter in Word, then read and edit every line. Hold fn to dictate the account note. Keep your payer's appeal rules open next to the draft.

faq.question: Is medical billing a shrinking job?
faq.answer: The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts 418,000 billing and posting clerks in 2025 and projects essentially no change through 2035. BLS does not list medical billers as their own group, so treat that as a close proxy.

painPoints.title: Software that does not fit your Mac
painPoints.text: Some billing systems are Windows programs. Tebra's desktop app is one of them, and its Mac option runs through a companion. You may end up juggling a Windows PC and a browser for the same claim.

painPoints.title: Denials that wait too long in a queue
painPoints.text: Unworked denials are the expensive part. Vendor sources cite about $25 per rework. Many denials sit in the queue because nobody has time to research them.

painPoints.title: Insurer calls and authorization checks
painPoints.text: Waiting on hold, then writing a reference number into a notes field, can eat a morning. Authorization checks add more calls to the same day.

painPoints.title: Retyping the same facts across screens
painPoints.text: The same claim facts get typed into claim software, a tracker, an email and an appeal letter. Every copy is a chance for a typo.

painPoints.title: Code and policy questions with no one to ask
painPoints.text: Payer policies change and code references update. A biller working alone needs an answer now, not next week.
